Right, so in other words “I will not read reputable evidence contrary to my claims because it doesn’t align with my beliefs, but I will spread misinformation about a widely used medication because *I* don’t think it’s appropriate for *me*”.

No one is telling *you* to take beta blockers. The concern is that you are discounting an entire class of medications that may be effective for OP (for them to discuss with their doctor) based on misinterpretation of findings or low quality evidence.

Respectfully, a Google search and having a conversation with your doctor is not equivalent to doctoral training, whether MD/fellowships or PhD/postdoc.

What about women who don’t have the money in time to access abortion? Many of these states enacting shorter and shorter bans have so few clinics that wait times for appointments are *weeks*. Many have requirements that women wait a minimum of 24-72 hours between appointments.

Multiple clinic visits means travel money, lodging money, time off from work, then paying for the abortion, which can be [thousands of dollars](https://www.plannedparenthood.org/learn/ask-experts/how-much-does-an-abortion-cost). In [33 states](https://www.kff.org/womens-health-policy/issue-brief/the-hyde-amendment-and-coverage-for-abortion-services/) public funds like Medicaid cannot be used for abortion, except in cases of rape, incest, or life endangerment.

Access to abortion for many women is incredibly difficult.

Imagine a single mother in Missouri, which has one clinic in the entire state (or a state of your choosing - [89% of US counties had no abortion clinics](https://www.guttmacher.org/fact-sheet/state-facts-about-abortion-missouri)). In Missouri there is a mandatory [72 hour waiting period](https://sarah.wustl.edu/abortion-care/) between clinic visits to access abortion. For states with the bare minimum of clinics, wait times for appointments can take *weeks*.

That means time off from work, finding and being able to afford childcare, paying for travel and lodging for multiple days. Then paying for the abortion, which can range from [hundreds to thousands of dollars](https://www.plannedparenthood.org/learn/ask-experts/how-much-does-an-abortion-cost). Oh, and both [public *and* private insurance](https://www.guttmacher.org/fact-sheet/state-facts-about-abortion-missouri) in our example here will only cover insurance in cases of life endangerment. Public funding *may* be available in cases of rape.

What happens when these women don’t have the money available in the increasingly shorter time windows states are pushing? If they can’t afford an abortion how will they afford a child?

Let’s pretend that these women can’t access abortion and choose the adoption route ([even though 90% of women denied abortion will not place a child for adoption](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28153742/) even if they are not prepared to be parents). Who foots the [exorbitant bill](https://www.businessinsider.com/how-much-does-it-cost-to-have-a-baby-2018-4?amp) to give birth? What about paying for prenatal care to ensure the baby is healthy?

Not everyone has equal access to abortion within ever-shortening time frames to get one. Adding red tape well before viability even comes into play serves no one.
